narrative.what_i_did:
The operator asked for the 'Your secrets' experience to stop living as a launcher card buried on the Identity tab and instead become an interactive dashboard inside the People tab, right where the messages and threads are — a 'dashboard condo' that expands out, shows all the secret cards you've made, lets you edit them, send pieces out individually, and offers every share channel available: Nostr, QR, AirDrop, 'tap whatever.' Before cutting I grounded against the actual code and found the whole dashboard already existed as components — SecretsLedgerList, SecretDetail, the create and recover and per-piece distribution flows — but trapped inside SharedSecretModal, a fixed overlay opened from the SharedSecretSection card on the Identity tab. The People tab (PeopleTabBody) already had a List/Tree toggle. So the work was a relocation and inline-ing, not a rewrite.

There was one real snag I refused to flip silently: the operator's words 'all the cards you've done and send out individual request from there' imply re-sending pieces from an existing card anytime, but the previous carpenter had made the ledger METADATA ONLY a load-bearing, test-guarded, prime-directive-cited choice — the share tokens are never persisted, so once you close out of a freshly-made secret the pieces are gone and re-sending means making the secret again. Honoring 'send from a card anytime' would require keeping the encrypted pieces on the device, reversing that deliberate rule. I surfaced that as a chip-form question alongside a placement question. The operator chose to STAY metadata-only (the rule holds), and for placement gave a custom answer: List and Tree visible always, Secrets collapses down and expands when needed. That settled the design precisely — not a third sibling tab that replaces List/Tree, but a collapsible card alongside them.

I extracted the modal body verbatim into SecretsDashboard.tsx, rendered inline with no modal chrome, no body-scroll lock, no Close button, and added a Share button over the existing Web Share API helper (shareText) that fires the iOS/PWA system share sheet — that is the real AirDrop/Messages/Mail channel — gated behind canShare() so it does not just duplicate Copy on desktop engines. True NFC 'tap' is not implemented anywhere in the wallet, so I leaned on the system sheet rather than faking a tap that does nothing. PeopleSecretsSection.tsx is the collapsible condo card; it owns open/close and lazy-loads the dashboard chunk on first expand so people who never open secrets pay nothing. I mounted it in PeopleTabBody right under the inbox, deleted the now-orphaned SharedSecretModal and SharedSecretSection, removed the Identity-tab mount so there is one integrated home not two, renamed the bundle-budget chunk pattern, and updated the recovery manifest's touches and note. All four gates green: typecheck, lint, 575 tests, build with budgets OK (SecretsDashboard measured 7.29KB gz under its 8.5KB budget).
narrative.whats_pending:
Zero device validation, as usual for this arc. The operator should open the People tab on the phone, confirm List and Tree still read as the always-visible default, expand the 'Your secrets' card, and walk the full loop: pick a scenario, make a secret, hand the pieces out over each channel — Send to a circle member over chat, Share via the system sheet (AirDrop/Messages), Copy, QR — tag who got each one, then bring a secret back by pasting a threshold subset. The thing to watch is whether the collapsible card reads as 'easy to get to and integrated' in the hand, and whether the five per-piece buttons (Send/Share/Copy/QR/Tag) wrap cleanly on a narrow screen — I added flex-wrap but it is unverified on a real device.

The metadata-only decision means an existing card still cannot re-send a piece; the operator chose that knowingly, but it is worth watching in field-test whether 'I made it, closed it, and now want to hand the last piece to one more person' feels like a gap. If it does, the captured fork is: persist the encrypted pieces (reverses the prime-directive line) versus keep make-again-to-redistribute. That is a live design question, not a bug.

The broader 'more later' roadmap is unchanged from the prior session: blind-custody, consensus-release ceremony, beneficiaries, then the two north stars — FROST threshold-signing and the Bitcoin tapscript inheritance vault — all captured in the 2026-06-04 conditional-release brief and the ideas.md thesis chain. The wider field-test backlog also still stands. The order-dependent identity-gate canonicalization test flake remains latent; it did not surface (suite green).
narrative.what_you_could_do_better: Nothing surfaced beyond the declared scope this session. The one judgment call worth naming honestly is that I removed the Identity-tab launcher entirely rather than leaving a pointer, on the reasoning that 'integrated not bolted on, not having to go somewhere else' argues for a single home and that the operator's recommended placement option was 'move fully into People.' The operator's actual answer redirected to the collapse/expand layout and did not explicitly bless removing the Identity card, so if they expected it to stay reachable from Identity too, that is a one-line revert. I called it the cleaner read and flagged it here so it is easy to reverse if wrong.
narrative.bigger_picture: This is the experience-is-the-moat thesis applied at the level of where a feature lives, not just how it reads. The previous session made the secrets primitive legible by fronting it with plain-language scenarios; this session made it reachable by putting it where a person already is — among their people and messages — instead of behind a card on a different tab. Nothing cryptographic changed; the Shamir core, the ledger, the templates are all untouched. What changed is proximity and integration: the secrets condo now sits next to the connections it depends on, because a jointly-held secret is fundamentally about the people who hold it. The collapsible-alongside-List/Tree shape the operator specified is itself a small lesson in not replacing what works — he did not want secrets to take over the People view, he wanted it to live there quietly and expand on demand. The share-channel addition follows the same honesty discipline the codebase already practices: I wired the real system share sheet (which is what AirDrop actually is on iOS) and explicitly did not fake an NFC tap that the wallet has no implementation for. The durable-UI-over-swappable-primitive frame keeps holding: every later cut — blind-custody, consensus-release, inheritance — now has an obvious home to grow into, as another template behind the same pick-configure-distribute-retrieve flow, now reachable from the tab where people actually spend their time.

questions_asked.question: To send pieces from an existing secret card anytime, the wallet has to keep the pieces; today it deliberately keeps only a record of where each piece went. Which way?
questions_asked.carpenters_read: The prime-directive line holds — tokens are never persisted. Re-send from an old card stays impossible by design; redistributing means making the secret again. The dashboard still has every share channel on the live create/distribute flow.

questions_asked.question: Where should the 'Your secrets' home live once the People -> Secrets tab exists?
questions_asked.operator_answered: Free-form: 'list and tree visible always and secrets collapse down expand when needed'
questions_asked.carpenters_read: Not a sibling tab that swaps with List/Tree, but a collapsible card alongside them that expands on demand. I read this as endorsing the single-home move and removed the Identity launcher; flagged as a one-line revert if they wanted it kept.

operator_directives: Secrets needs its own place inside People where the messages are — an interactive dashboard 'condo' that expands out, shows all the cards you've made, lets you edit them and send out pieces individually, with all the features right there.
Make it nice and pretty, easy to get to, integrated not bolted on.
Offer all the share options available — Nostr, QR, AirDrop, tap whatever.
List and Tree visible always; Secrets collapses down and expands when needed.
Stay metadata-only — do not start keeping the pieces.

feedback_to_appcommander: Clean small relocation cut with one genuine prime-directive tension, handled the way the doctrine wants: I did not silently reverse the previous carpenter's load-bearing metadata-only decision to satisfy a literal reading of the operator's request — I surfaced the tradeoff as a chip-form question and built to the answer. Two skeleton-worthy patterns reinforced here. First, when a new request collides with a deliberate, test-guarded invariant from a prior session, the right move is to name the collision in chip form, not to either ignore the request or quietly flip the invariant. Second, the 'integrated not bolted on' instinct kept paying off: the dashboard already existed as components, so the cut was relocation and inline-ing, and recognizing that before reaching for new code is exactly the grounding-gate discipline. The honesty note about NFC — refusing to add a fake 'tap' affordance because the wallet has no NFC implementation, and instead wiring the real system share sheet — is the kind of small integrity call worth keeping visible in the comms record.
